title: What is GitHub Pages, and Why Should Academics Care?
author: Academic Visuals Initiative

content.credit: Photo by Mohammad Rahmani on Pexels

content.text: At its core, GitHub Pages is a hosting service designed to publish static websites directly from a GitHub repository. While widely used by software developers, it is also a highly practical tool for academics, researchers, and graduate students. By hosting your website on GitHub, you can manage your research portfolio, teaching materials, and professional CV in a single, stable location without relying on institutional web systems.

GitHub Pages functions by serving static web files—such as HTML, CSS, and plain text files written in Markdown—stored in your repository. To launch a site, you simply create a repository, upload your files, and enable GitHub Pages in the repository's settings. Within minutes, your site is publicly accessible.

For academics who may not have web development experience, the process is often simplified by using pre-built templates designed specifically for scholars (such as AcademicPages). Additionally, built-in integration with Jekyll (a static site generator) allows you to write your CV, blog posts, or research updates in plain text (Markdown), which the system automatically formats into a clean, professional website.
Key Benefits for Academics and Graduate Students
Unlike commercial hosting platforms, GitHub Pages is entirely free. This makes it an accessible option for graduate students, postdocs, and early-career researchers operating on limited budgets.

Institutional profile pages are tied to your current employment. If you transition to a new university, your page is often deleted. A GitHub Pages site belongs to you and remains your permanent academic home throughout your career, regardless of your institutional affiliation.

Because your website lives in a GitHub repository, every change you make is tracked. If you are co-authoring a project website or co-teaching a course, multiple collaborators can easily update the site using GitHub's built-in collaboration features.

Since static sites do not use databases, they are highly secure and require virtually no administrative maintenance. You do not need to worry about software updates, database crashes, or security plugins, allowing you to focus on your research.
You can easily connect a custom domain (e.g., yourname.com) to your site, and GitHub automatically provides an SSL certificate to ensure a secure connection.
Because GitHub Pages only hosts static files (meaning it does not support dynamic databases or server-side languages like PHP), it is highly optimized for the following academic formats:

items: Personal Portfolios and CVs: A central, customizable hub to share your publications, teaching philosophy, biography, and contact information.
Lab or Research Group Websites: A cost-effective way to present team members, current projects, and publication lists without requiring departmental funding or IT approval.
Course Websites: A stable, easily updated platform for hosting course syllabi, lecture slides, assignment sheets, and reading lists.
Supplementary Research Materials: A place to host project updates, white papers, or supplementary data required by funding agencies.

Interactive Research and Data Demos: Researchers working with R, Python, or Julia can easily publish static HTML reports (such as R Markdown or Jupyter notebooks) to share reproducible data visualizations and methodologies.

content.text: GitHub Pages offers a reliable, zero-cost, and portable solution for publishing academic content. By integrating web hosting with version control, it allows researchers and graduate students to maintain full ownership of their professional identity and research output over the long term.
